articles.title: BepiColombo begins Mercury arrival with MTM separation success
articles.description: On 3 September 2026 at 15:49 CEST, the European Space Agency's BepiColombo Mission Control Team at the European Space Operations Centre (ESOC) received the signal they had been waiting for – BepiColombo’s Mercury Transfer Module (MTM) successfully separated from the spacecraft stack. This landmark achievement for the ESA and Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) mission marks the first step of BepiColombo's long-awaited arrival at Mercury.
articles.summary: ESA's BepiColombo successfully completes MTM separation maneuver on September 3, 2026, marking the beginning of its arrival phase at Mercury after eight years of travel. This major milestone brings the mission closer to detailed scientific observations of the solar system's innermost planet.

articles.title: Roman lifts off on a mission to survey the infrared sky
articles.description:
Image:
			
NASA’s Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope lifted off on a SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket from NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida, USA, at 07:26 EDT / 12:26 BST/ 13:26 CEST on 30 August 2026. With the successful launch, Roman began its mission to survey the sky in visible to near-infrared light to help reveal the nature of dark energy and dark matter. The telescope will also investigate the true diversity of exoplanets in our galaxy.
Roman is a NASA-led mission to which the European Space Agency (ESA) contributed star trackers, batteries, and detectors for the coronagraph instrument. ESA will also provide communications support through its deep-space ground station network, and enable data download using its new 35-metre antenna in New Norcia, Australia.
“I warmly congratulate our colleagues at NASA on the successful launch of Roman,” says Carole Mundell, ESA’s Director of Science. “ESA is proud to have provided essential hardware and to continue supporting Roman’s ambitious scientific goals. Together, we are opening new windows on the cosmos.”
Like ESA’s Euclid space telescope, Roman will enable astronomers to study the Universe in unprecedented detail. It is equipped with a primary mirror of 2.4 m and two instruments: the Wide Field Instrument (WFI) and a Coronagraph Instrument technology demonstration.
With its panoramic view of the sky, crisp infrared vision and quick re-orientation skills, Roman will perform fast and efficient surveys of a large area of the sky. By doing so, it will map clustering of galaxies over time and space and also study the light coming from thousands of distant type Ia supernovas which will help astronomers trace the expansion of the Universe.
“Roman should provide our clearest picture yet of whether dark energy is truly constant or whether it evolves over cosmic time – either outcome would have profound implications for our understanding of the Universe. I'm also excited by Roman's exoplanet census, which will discover thousands of new worlds, including cold planets and free-floating planets that have remained largely beyond our reach until now,” says Bethan James, ESA’s Roman Project Scientist. “Perhaps what excites me most is the unexpected. With its unprecedented combination of depth, area, and image quality, Roman has every opportunity to surprise us.”
After launch, Roman is on a steady course to the second Sun-Earth Lagrange point (L2), nearly 1.5 million km away from Earth. This location allows the telescope to have an unobstructed view of a wide area of the sky, almost 12%. Like ESA’s Euclid and the NASA/ESA/CSA James Webb Space Telescope, Roman will move in a wider orbit around the L2 point – much larger than the Moon’s orbit around Earth.
In the next three months following launch, the Roman team will conduct a carefully orchestrated series of deployments, calibrations, and tests. Once the commissioning period is complete, the mission will begin its science operations, starting with the first science image release. Roman will spend at least five years scanning the infrared sky and is designed to work in space for another five years.
[Image description: A SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket with NASA’s Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope on board is seen transiting the Sun during launch from Launch Complex 39A, on Sunday 30 August 2026, at NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida, US.]
articles.summary: NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope successfully launches aboard a SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket from Kennedy Space Center to begin its infrared sky survey mission. This landmark mission will advance humanity's understanding of dark energy, exoplanets, and distant galaxies.

articles.title: A New Catalog of Close to 3,000 Supernova Challenges Theories on Dark Energy
articles.description: The most comprehensive catalogue of exploding white dwarf stars ever assembled has revealed new clues about dark energy, the mysterious force driving the universe’s accelerating expansion.
articles.summary: A comprehensive catalog of nearly 3,000 supernova observations provides unprecedented insights into dark energy and challenges existing cosmological theories. This major dataset advances our understanding of the universe's expansion and fundamental physics.

articles.title: NASA's next great observatory could spot oceans on distant worlds
articles.description: We've found more than 5,500 exoplanets so far. Dozens of them are in the habitable zones of their parent stars, where, at least in theory, they could host an ocean. But we've never definitively found a liquid ocean on another planet.
articles.source: Space News - Space, Astronomy, Space Exploration
articles.summary: A next-generation NASA observatory will have unprecedented capability to detect water and assess habitability on distant exoplanets. This transformative technology promises breakthrough discoveries in the search for potentially habitable worlds.

articles.title: Researchers pinpoint key early-universe measurement with record precision
articles.description: An international team, including researchers from the University of Minnesota Twin Cities, has reached a major milestone in "precision cosmology" by measuring the amount of helium created in the universe's first five minutes with unprecedented accuracy.
articles.source: Space News - Space, Astronomy, Space Exploration
articles.summary: Researchers achieved record-breaking precision in measuring a fundamental early-universe parameter, advancing our understanding of cosmic origins. This international milestone refines our knowledge of how the universe began and evolved.

articles.description:
Nearly five decades after launch, humanity's most distant emissary continues whispering back from the edge of the solar system, defying every expectation of how long a machine can survive in the void.
The post On 5 September 1977 Voyager 1 left Cape Canaveral…
articles.summary: Nearly 47 years after launch, Voyager 1 continues its extraordinary journey at 164.7 AU from Earth, still transmitting data and serving as humanity's most distant emissary. This mission represents an unparalleled testament to engineering longevity and our exploration of the outer solar system.

articles.title: Breaking: Starship's Biggest Flight Yet Is Just Days Away! [23:31]
articles.description: SpaceX's Starship Flight 14 has a launch window, and a Starship is back at the launch pad with a surprising twist! We dive into plans for Starlink V3 deployment, Ship 42's catch-system tests, Super Heavy Booster 22's cryogenic testing, and major upgrades at S…
articles.summary: SpaceX's Starship Flight 14 is imminent with a confirmed launch window, featuring a fully stacked vehicle returning to the pad with exciting new modifications. This milestone represents another landmark test of humanity's most powerful reusable launch system.

articles.title: Hubble's superbubble scene
articles.description:
Image:
			
This sprawling cosmic vista and subject of today’s ESA/Hubble Picture of the Month comes from the Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC). The LMC is the largest of the small galaxies that orbit our Milky Way galaxy. At just 160 000 light-years away, the LMC offers a close look at highly active stellar birthsites like the nebula shown here. This nebula is named LHA 120-N44, or N44 for short, and it’s located in the constellation Dorado.
The appearance of this photogenic nebula is dominated by two features: a vast central void and a shell of dense, dusty gas. The central void is a ‘superbubble’ spanning roughly 210 by 140 light-years. The glittering stars at the centre of the void are responsible for its creation; through their powerful stellar winds and explosive supernovae, these stars have expelled much of the gas from which they were born.
When the stars of N44’s central star cluster swept away this gas, the expelled gas formed a shell around the superbubble. New stars are forming in this compressed gas shell, making N44 an interesting target for researchers studying the process of star formation. In particular, astronomers have turned to this nebula as an ideal place to time this process from start to finish. Their goal is to understand how long it takes from the collapse of cold gas clouds into dense knots to the moment nuclear fusion ignites in the heart of a newborn star.
Researchers used Hubble to survey N44 and take a census of its stars, cataloguing nearly half a million stars within the cluster as well as interlopers drifting in front of it. Of the stars surveyed, nearly 30 000 are what astronomers call pre-main-sequence stars, which have yet to begin fusing hydrogen into helium in their cores. This treasure trove of baby stars was discoverable thanks to the high sensitivity and fine spatial resolution of Hubble’s instruments that can pick out faint objects in crowded clusters.
The gas shell surrounding the superbubble is energised by ultraviolet radiation from massive stars, causing it to glow and highlighting several distinct features. Each feature within the broader N44 star-forming complex was catalogued by astronomer Karl Henize in the 1950s. One feature is a smaller bubble, catalogued as N44F, that is located near the upper-right corner of this image. N44F is an interstellar bubble blown by the intense stellar winds of a single hot and massive star. As this previously released Hubble closeup shows, the star’s furious winds and radiation have sculpted the surrounding bubble and created pillars of dusty gas.
The data used to create this image come from an observing programme (#14689; PI: Gouliermis) that aimed to probe stars in the N44 complex that have not yet begun fusing hydrogen into heavier elements in their cores. These data help to determine how long the process of star formation takes, as well as what masses newborn stars typically have. Hubble's sensitive observations of the lowest-mass stars in this region open a new window onto star formation in regions that, like the LMC or the galaxies of the early Universe, are poor in elements heavier than helium.
[Image Description: A dense field of stars fills the image, surrounded by wispy clouds of gas and dust. Pale blue and grey nebulosity forms an intricate web across the scene, with darker clouds of dust concentrated towards the lower right. Numerous bright stars appear in shades of blue, white and orange.]
articles.summary: Hubble Space Telescope captures a striking image of a superbubble cosmic structure in the Large Magellanic Cloud, showcasing stellar phenomena and the beauty of the universe. This observation exemplifies Hubble's ongoing contribution to our understanding of stellar nurseries and cosmic structures.

articles.title: Hubble tracks new decagon encircling Saturn’s south pole
articles.description: Recent observations with the NASA/ESA Hubble Space Telescope have revealed a giant, evolving 10-sided atmospheric wave encircling Saturn’s south pole. This discovery marks the first time a large regular-sided jet pattern has been observed in the planet’s southern hemisphere. The feature appears remarkably similar to Saturn’s famous hexagon at its northern pole, but is also distinctly different, suggesting scientists may be witnessing a new atmospheric phenomenon develop on the iconic gas giant.
articles.summary: NASA/ESA Hubble Space Telescope reveals a giant 10-sided atmospheric wave pattern encircling Saturn's south pole in recent observations. This discovery provides new insights into the complex atmospheric dynamics of the gas giant.

articles.title: A New Design For A Plasma Engine Fuels On Only Thin Air
articles.description: Choosing what orbit to put a satellite in always comes with trade-offs. When it comes to Very Low Earth Orbit (VLEO), between 100-450 km, there are distinct advantages. Remote sensing cameras can take better pictures, comms and radar require less power, and atmospheric drag will automatically clean up dead satellites. But there’s also a cost - air friction requires any satellite in this orbit to use an engine near constantly to stay in orbit, which in turn requires fuel - typically in the form of expensive gases like Xenon. So, as part of his PhD thesis at the University of Stuttgart, which is available in arXiv, Francesco Romano decided to solve that problem by using the very air molecules that cause that friction as fuel for a plasma engine to keep satellites aloft indefinitely in VLEO.
articles.summary: A groundbreaking new plasma engine design achieves fuel efficiency by operating on thin air, enabling satellites to maintain very low Earth orbits. This innovation promises to extend mission lifespans and reduce operational costs for future space missions.

articles.title: Dense Galaxies Are Carving Out A Bubble in the Early Universe
articles.description: Light could only travel freely in the Universe after cosmic reionization. Before that, neutral hydrogen stopped photons from travelling. The JWST has found evidence of an overdensity of galaxies carving out a bubble of reionization. Is this how it all started?
articles.summary: Dense galaxies in the early universe are discovered carving out bubbles of ionized gas, advancing understanding of cosmic reionization. This discovery sheds light on how the first galaxies transformed the universe after the cosmic dark ages.

articles.title: How Big Can The Universe's First Starbursts Get?
articles.description: As our telescopes have improved and we’ve been able to peer farther back in time, we’ve begun finding more fascinating features of the universe. But one thing we definitely haven’t found yet is Population III (Pop III) stars. These were the earliest stars in the universe, formed completely from pristine hydrogen and helium, with no “metals” (i.e. elements heavier than those two) polluting their processes. They are also theorized to be absolutely massive, and “die with passion” as Bill Wurtz once put it in a famous YouTube video. A new paper, available in pre-print form on arXiv by Tae Bong Jeon from the Cosmic Frontier Center at the University of Texas at Austin, looks at just how massive those starbursts could be, and whether the James Webb Space Telescope could detect one.
articles.summary: Improved telescopes reveal increasingly massive starburst galaxies in the early universe, challenging models of the largest possible stellar birth events. These discoveries expand our understanding of the universe's most extreme and energetic cosmic phenomena.

articles.title: What's Carving Active Gullies on Mars? It's Not Water
articles.description: Scientists were shocked when they received the first images of Martian gullies. They were even more shocked as those gullies appeared to change over time. Their similarities to gullies seen on Earth were uncanny, but all of Earth’s gullies are formed by the water run-off, and Martian is too cold and has too sparse an atmosphere to have liquid water on its surface. Whatever has been causing those changing gullies couldn’t have been water, so what was it? A new paper from Apolline Leclef of the Institut d’Astrophysique Spatiale at Université Paris-Saclay and her colleagues, available in pre-print on arXiv, shows how they are likely caused by CO2 frost turning into a fluid.
articles.summary: Scientists investigate the mechanisms creating active gullies on Mars, revealing surprising findings about planetary geology. New imaging data challenges previous assumptions about Martian surface processes.

articles.title: Gravitational-wave analysis narrows the search for black hole impostors
articles.description: Black holes are regions of spacetime where gravity is so strong that nothing, not even light, can escape. When two black holes orbit each other and merge, they produce gravitational waves (i.e., ripples in spacetime) that can resemble those emitted by mergers involving other exotic compact objects.
articles.source: Space News - Space, Astronomy, Space Exploration
articles.summary: Gravitational-wave analysis provides new tools to distinguish genuine black holes from other compact objects. This advancement refines our ability to study extreme cosmic phenomena.

articles.title: Japan's Hayabusa2 achieves first-ever laser ranging experiment with an asteroid
articles.description: The Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency's (JAXA) Hayabusa2 spacecraft reached another milestone this summer, a first for space agencies. On Sunday, July 5, the probe conducted the first successful laser-ranging experiment during a flyby of asteroid Torifune, the first exploration target of Hayabusa2's Extended Mission. This latest milestone will advance the capabilities of JAXA and other space agencies as they pursue future missions involving near-Earth asteroids (NEAs) and other deep-space objects.
articles.source: Space News - Space, Astronomy, Space Exploration
articles.summary: JAXA's Hayabusa2 spacecraft successfully conducted the first-ever laser ranging experiment on an asteroid. This technological achievement opens new possibilities for asteroid science and future space missions.

articles.title: Rubin observatory peers deep into the famous COSMOS field
articles.description: The COSMOS field, or Cosmic Evolution Survey Deep Field, is one of the most famous patches of the universe observed by astronomers. Located in the constellation Sextans, this region was photographed by the Hubble Space Telescope (HST) in segments from 2003 to 2005 using its Advanced Camera for Surveys (ACS). With support from ground-based and other space-based telescopes, the resulting images were then stitched together to create a stunning picture of cosmic evolution.
articles.source: Space News - Space, Astronomy, Space Exploration
articles.summary: The Rubin observatory captures unprecedented deep observations of the famous COSMOS field, revealing new cosmic structures and phenomena. This data promises remarkable discoveries about galaxy evolution and universe composition.

articles.title: The Moon may have formed intact just hours after a giant collision
articles.description: Scientists have discovered that the Moon-forming collision may have depended heavily on how hot and physically strong early Earth and Theia were. New simulations found that some impacts create the familiar disk of debris that later becomes the Moon, while others can produce an intact Moon in only about five hours. The results challenge the long-standing assumption that the enormous collision could be modeled as if both worlds behaved mostly like fluids.
articles.summary: New research indicates the Moon formed remarkably quickly, potentially within hours of the giant impact that created it. This discovery transforms our understanding of the Moon's formation and early Solar System history.

articles.title: Interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS is bursting with methanol
articles.description: Interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS contains exceptionally high levels of methanol, suggesting it formed under conditions very different from those that shaped most comets in our solar system. ALMA also revealed that tiny icy grains around the comet are releasing methanol like miniature comets, giving astronomers an unusually detailed look at an object from another star system.
articles.summary: Interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS contains exceptionally high levels of methanol, providing insights into the conditions under which it formed in a distant stellar system.

articles.title: James Webb Space Telescope discovers the rings of tiny solar system body Chariklo are changing
articles.description: Using the James Webb Space Telescope, astronomers have discovered that the ring system of the tiny solar system body is even more interesting than they knew.
articles.summary: The James Webb Space Telescope has discovered that the ring system of the tiny solar system body Chariklo is undergoing dynamic changes, revealing new insights into planetary ring systems.

articles.title: A Cosmic Catastrophe May Have Turned Neptune’s Ancient Moons Inside Out
articles.description: This image of the Neptune system, captured by the Near-Infrared Camera (NIRCam) on NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope in 2022, reveals stunning views of the planet’s rings—which have not been seen with this clarity in more than three decades—along with the pla…
articles.summary: A cosmic catastrophe may have dramatically altered Neptune's ancient moons, with James Webb Space Telescope observations providing new evidence for understanding the gas giant's moon system.

articles.title: Four amateur astronomers using a telescope in Chile’s Atacama desert found a comet on 13 January 2026, 81 days before it would graze past the Sun. Nobody alive had seen its previous pass, because the orbit it travels on brings it back only about every 1,900 years.
articles.description:
A glimpse of a celestial wanderer that last visited during the Middle Ages—caught not by professional observatories, but by four amateurs with a telescope and patience.
The post Four amateur astronomers using a telescope in Chile’s Atacama desert found a come…
articles.summary: Four amateur astronomers in Chile's Atacama Desert discovered a rare comet 81 days before its closest approach to the Sun, with an orbital period of approximately 1,900 years—a remarkable feat of citizen science.

articles.title: Icy Exocomets Around a Distant Star Help Explain Earth's Water
articles.description: Did icy comets deliver water to the young Earth? That idea won't go away. Now, astronomers at Lund University in Sweden have found evidence of exocomets orbiting a young star named PDS 70. The observations suggest that these comets are delivering water to tha…
articles.summary: Astronomers discover icy exocomets around a distant star, providing new evidence that cometary delivery may explain the origins of Earth's water. This finding strengthens our understanding of how life-supporting oceans formed on our planet.

articles.title: Astronomy Picture of the Day - Hubble: Decagon Around Saturn's South Pole
articles.description: Explanation: Why are Saturn’s poles geometric? Saturn’s North Pole has been known to be surrounded by a hexagonal (6 sides) cloud since discovery in 1987 in data taken by NASA’s Voyager spacecrafts, which quickly flew past the ringed world in the early 1980s.…
articles.summary: The Hubble Space Telescope reveals a striking geometric decagon (10-sided pattern) circling Saturn's south pole, joining the famous hexagonal formation at its north pole. This discovery showcases Saturn's extraordinary atmospheric dynamics and offers rare insights into planetary wave mechanics.

articles.title: NASA Scientists Discover Giant 10-Sided Pattern on Saturn’s South Pole
articles.description: NASA’s Hubble Space Telescope has detected a massive, evolving 10-sided atmospheric wave circling Saturn’s south pole, according to a study published Sept. 3, 2026, in the journal Science Advances. The finding, reported by NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center, …
articles.summary: NASA's Hubble Space Telescope detects a massive, evolving 10-sided atmospheric wave at Saturn's south pole, a rare phenomenon that gives scientists an unprecedented opportunity to study unusual atmospheric patterns. This discovery adds to our understanding of giant planet meteorology.

articles.title: China Plans To Return Samples From Mars In 2031 After The U.S. Cancels Its Own Plans
articles.description: The Chinese mission to Mars is on pace to launch in 2028, and it may beat the U.S. back to Earth with soil samples, even though the U.S. is already there.
articles.summary: China's ambitious Mars sample-return mission is progressing toward a 2028 launch, positioning the nation to potentially return Martian soil samples before the United States. This represents a major milestone in international Mars exploration and sample-return science.

articles.title: From Larissa to space: The journey of Adrianos Golemis, Greece’s first astronaut
articles.description:
The Greek scientist who cared for the health of ESA crews is now preparing to fly himself to the International Space Station
The post From Larissa to space: The journey of Adrianos Golemis, Greece’s first astronaut appeared first on ProtoThema English.
articles.summary: Adrianos Golemis, Greece's first astronaut and a distinguished ESA space medicine expert, is preparing to fly to the International Space Station. His journey represents a historic achievement for Greece and celebrates the international spirit of space exploration.

articles.title: The Moon is airless, radiation-drenched and can swing from about minus 173 to plus 127 degrees Celsius, yet NASA-led modelling found that some common Earth fungi and bacteria—from human skin, soil and damp bathrooms—could survive dormant for weeks or even months in cold, shaded niches near the lunar poles.
articles.description:
A NASA-led model identifies cold lunar south-pole shadows where terrestrial fungi and bacteria may remain dormant for days and, in especially protected conditions, longer.
The post The Moon is airless, radiation-drenched and can swing from about minus 173 to …
articles.summary: NASA-led modeling reveals that common Earth microorganisms could potentially survive dormant in cold, shaded lunar south-pole niches for extended periods. This finding has profound implications for understanding microbial resilience and future lunar habitability research.

articles.title: L’Europe veut enfin son « Dragon » : un contrat record de 760 millions pour une jeune entreprise cofondée par une Française
articles.description: L'Agence spatiale européenne a signé, lors du Sommet de l'espace à Paris, son plus important contrat de transport spatial avec une entreprise franco-allemande. La capsule Nyx de The Exploration Company, en cours de développement, doit désormais s'amarrer à l'…
articles.summary: The European Space Agency awards a record 760-million-euro contract to a young space transport company co-founded by a French entrepreneur, marking Europe's major step toward developing its own commercial launch capability. This partnership strengthens European independence in space transportation.

articles.title: Could the Clues to Ancient Alien Civilizations Be Hiding in a Bucket of Moon Dust?
articles.description: Most of our experience with the Search for Extraterrestrial Intelligence (SETI) has been focused on capturing radio signals that alien species have sent out, whether intentionally or unintentionally. That creates a huge “synchronicity” problem - what if there aren’t any alien civilizations broadcasting radio signals now, but there were a billion years ago? The Milky Way is around 13 billion years old - hoping that we exist at the same time as an alien civilization that happens to be actively messaging is a huge leap of faith. But, according to a new paper available in pre-print on arXiv and submitted to the International Journal of Astrobiology by Lewis J Pinault, as associated researcher at the SETI Institute, and his co-authors, we could take a completely alternative approach to trying to find alien civilizations - by looking for evidence of them in lunar dirt.
articles.summary: Scientists explore how lunar dust samples could reveal evidence of ancient extraterrestrial civilizations, expanding SETI research beyond traditional radio signal detection. This innovative approach combines lunar science with the search for extraterrestrial intelligence.

articles.title: Venus Moon Would Have Been Doomed From The Start, Says New Paper
articles.description: Venus likely never had a moon and even if it did, it would have soon been torn asunder by the planet’s own gravity, says prominent planetary astrophysicist.
articles.summary: New research suggests Venus likely never possessed a moon due to the planet's powerful gravitational forces that would have destroyed any natural satellite. This finding provides insights into planetary formation and the unique characteristics of our solar system.
